candidates.title: Robotic manipulation datasets for offline compositional reinforcement learning
candidates.description: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising direction that allows RL agents to be pre-trained from large datasets avoiding recurrence of expensive data collection. To advance the field, it is crucial to generate large-scale datasets. Compositional RL is particularly appealing for generating such large datasets, since 1) it permits creating many tasks from few components, and 2) the task structure may enable trained agents to solve new tasks by combining relevant learned components. This submission provides four offline RL datasets for simulated robotic manipulation created using the 256 tasks from CompoSuite [Mendez et al., 2022] ( https://github.com/Lifelong-ML/CompoSuite ). In every task in CompoSuite, a *robot* arm is used to manipulate an *object* to achieve an *objective* all while trying to avoid an *obstacle*. There are for components for each of these four axes that can be combined arbitrarily leading to a total of 256 tasks. The component choices are * Robot: IIWA, Jaco, Kinova3, Panda * Object: Hollow box, box, dumbbell, plate * Objective: Push, pick and place, put in shelf, put in trashcan * Obstacle: None, wall between robot and object, wall between goal and object, door between goal and object The four included datasets are collected using separate agents each trained to a different degree of performance, and each dataset consists of 256 million transitions. The degrees of performance are expert data, medium data, warmstart data and replay data: * Expert dataset: Transitions from an expert agent that was trained to achieve 90% success on every task. * Medium dataset: Transitions from a medium agent that was trained to achieve 30% success on every task. * Warmstart dataset: Transitions from a Soft-actor critic agent trained for a fixed duration of one million steps. * Medium-replay-subsampled dataset: Transitions that were stored during the training of a medium agent up to 30% success. These datasets are intended for the combined study of compositional generalization and offline reinforcement learning.

candidates.title: SNP dataset for cape race brook trout
candidates.description: Many studies have investigated the loss of adaptive potential in endangered or exploited species experiencing recent population declines. Less research has studied adaptive genomic variation in small populations known to have persisted for long periods, despite the unique contribution that such populations provide for determining mechanisms underlying population persistence in evolutionary and conservation modeling. Small populations of Brook trout ( Salvelinus fontinalis ) have persisted in Cape Race, Newfoundland for >12,000 years. We used genotyping-by-sequencing data to investigate the demographic history and adaptive genomic variation of 26 populations with effective population sizes (N e ) ranging from 11 to 442, and to explore mechanisms underlying long-term persistence. We show that all populations experienced demographic declines following postglacial colonization but have remained in their current, small N e state for thousands of years. We also reveal greater homozygosity in adaptive alleles within the smallest populations and found signatures of adaptive divergence in small populations relating to several abiotic and biotic factors. Our study illustrates how the demographic history of a species can influence the adaptive dynamics of small populations persisting over long time periods.

candidates.title: The Málaga 2009 Robotic Dataset Collection: outdoor datasets with centimeter-accuracy ground truth (MRPT rawlog and ROS 2 MCAP)
candidates.description: Six outdoor datasets (PARKING-0L, PARKING-2L, PARKING-6L, CAMPUS-0L, CAMPUS-2L and CAMPUS-RT) recorded in November 2008 at the University of Málaga (Spain) with an electric vehicle equipped with three SICK and two Hokuyo laser scanners, two color cameras, an Xsens IMU, three RTK GPS receivers and one consumer-grade GPS receiver. A centimeter-level 6D ground truth of the vehicle path, with its uncertainty, is computed from the RTK GPS data, which makes the collection suitable as a test bed for visual SLAM, 2D SLAM, visual odometry and localization. Reference 3D point clouds built from the lasers are also provided. Each sequence is available as its original 2009 package (ZIP with the MRPT rawlog, raw and rectified images, ground truth and point clouds, byte-identical to the original release) and, since 2026, as a ROS 2 bag in MCAP format with the same sensor data and the ground truth, playable in ROS 2 Humble and newer and in Foxglove. See README.md for the list of topics. Web page: https://w3.ual.es/~jlblanco/datasets/malaga-2009-dataset/

candidates.title: TrollLabs Open Dataset
candidates.description: The TrollLabs Open dataset is the result of running a prototyping hackathon with the aim of elucidating the capabilities and performance of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, in the early stages of engineering design by comparing its performance to experienced engineering students in a hackathon setting. The dataset comprises 116 prototype entries and 433 edges(connection) that allows for comparative analysis of design practices, decisions and performance between one team instructed solely by generative AI, and five teams consisting of experienced engineering design students. Complementary, the dataset contains a copy of the chat between ChatGPT and the team tasked with executing its suggestions containing 41 prompts and answers. It contains the initial prompt used to instruct the AI, the objective and rules of the hackathon and the performance of teams, showing the ChatGPT team finishing 2nd among a total of six teams. The online prototype capture platform Pro2booth was used to collect comprehensive information about prototypes created and teams overall design processes. The data is particularly relevant to design researchers, engineering and design students, educators, and industry professionals seeking to find strategies for implementing or to implement generative AI tools in their design processes.

This dataset transcribes the Bodleian Libraries copy, Sinica 1798, including Chinese and English prefaces, medicine entries and bilingual name tables, for research on late-Qing medical translation, pharmaceutical terminology, medical missions and print. It covers 197 targeted physical faces in 104 digital captures, with source-linked TXT, JSON, TEI XML, uncertainty and layout-part records. This AI-assisted revision follows a separate source-image reading, page-by-page comparison and checking against the source images. Unresolved readings and exact encodings remain marked. Full human double collation and expert review have not been performed; see Methods.

candidates.title: Dataset on the Use of Bibliometric Indicators in Science Policy and Research Evaluation
candidates.description: Dataset comprising 116 peer-reviewed articles analysed in a study on the use of bibliometric indicators in science policy and research evaluation. The original corpus of 73 articles was expanded through a retrospective reassessment of the initial Scopus search results, incorporating 43 additional studies. The dataset includes descriptive and analytical variables covering study objectives, relationships with science and technology policy (STP), bibliometric indicators, main findings, conclusions, author affiliation countries, geographic scope, data sources, document types and temporal coverage. It also includes context-specific families of study objectives and a classification into four analytical systems: Descriptive, Evaluative, Structural/Analytical and Strategic/Normative. Bibliometric indicators are classified into four non-mutually exclusive dimensions — Production, Impact, Relational and Thematic — distinguishing indicators applied, mentioned without application, absent or undetermined. The original analytical summaries of the 73 articles were preserved, while summaries for 42 additional full-text articles were prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by the authors. One article, available only as an abstract, remains unclassified in analyses requiring full-text examination. The dataset includes a data dictionary documenting the variables, classification criteria and coding conventions. The articles were retrieved through a Scopus search combining "science policy" with bibliometric and scientometric terms, followed by a retrospective reassessment of the original search results.

candidates.title: Hardware-Rooted Protected Execution-Finality Using Scoped Non-Bearer Capabilities and Fail-Closed Finality Sinks
candidates.description: Detailed abstract A hardware-rooted or cryptographically enforced method and system prevent a proposed operation from producing an external effect until that exact operation is validated, bound, and admitted at a non-bypassable effectuation boundary. The proposed operation is first held as a Candidate Act in a non-effective hold state. A machine-verifiable act descriptor is established for the Candidate Act. Within a protected enforcement domain or protected enforcement path—such as a trusted execution environment, hardware security module, secure element, secure processor, SmartNIC, data-processing unit, memory controller, or other isolated circuitry—a set of machine-verifiable authority predicates is evaluated from the descriptor. A corresponding protected-state operation is performed, producing or referencing a protected-state representation. Protected validation evidence recording at least the predicate-validation outcome and the protected-state condition is committed before, or atomically with, authorization of a scoped non-bearer capability. The scoped non-bearer capability is cryptographically or machine-verifiably bound to the Candidate Act, the act descriptor or a digest thereof, the committed validation evidence, the protected-state representation, the execution-finality boundary, an applicable Finality Sink, a freshness constraint, and a permitted effectuation scope. Possession of the capability alone is insufficient: it is not a bearer token, API key, OAuth token, session cookie, or transferable credential. A copied, replayed, substituted, or re-presented instance fails when used for a different act, digest, sink, nonce, policy epoch, protected state, or scope. At or before the execution-finality boundary, the Finality Sink performs a machine-enforced capability-validity check and permits the Candidate Act to become externally effective only when the capability is validly bound to all required elements. Otherwise the system fails closed and the Candidate Act remains non-effective. In conventional terminology: Candidate Act ≈ staged command / pending transaction / transaction intent / prepared operation. The usefulness of the terminology is that a conventional word such as “request” can sometimes refer to something already transmitted or submitted. Candidate Act expressly identifies a state in which: the operation exists, but its consequence does not yet exist. 2. Non-Effective Hold State The non-effective hold state is the state in which the Candidate Act remains before release. It means: The operation has been computed or prepared, but some mechanism prevents it from yet producing the protected consequence. This resembles the prepare stage in transactional systems. For example: Database UPDATE balance ... The update may have been constructed but is not yet committed. Network A message may have been constructed in memory but not yet transmitted through the NIC. Robot MOVE_ARM(x=20,y=15) The command may have been generated, but the motor-control signal remains inhibited. Accordingly: non-effective hold state ≈ staged / prepared / pre-commit / interlocked state. 3. Execution-Finality Boundary The execution-finality boundary identifies the point separating: something the computer intends to do from something that has actually become consequential. The specific boundary varies by technology. Domain Possible execution-finality boundary Network NIC/DPU transmission or egress Storage persistent write or commit Memory protected memory commit GPU/NPU accelerator output or egress Payment ledger or value-transfer commit Telecom RF transmission Satellite command or actuator interface Robot motor or actuator controller Power system switching or enable interface Data disclosure interface that actually releases protected bytes In conventional systems literature, this may be called the: side-effect boundary, commit point, actuation boundary, egress boundary, or irreversible-operation boundary. The claim generalizes those domain-specific boundaries under a common architectural concept. 4. Finality Sink The Finality Sink is not simply another authorization server. It is the enforcement component controlling the actual consequence. In ordinary industry terminology, depending on the implementation, it may correspond functionally to a: reference monitorpolicy enforcement point (PEP)command gateactuation gatetransaction commit gateegress enforcement pointsafety interlock An important additional condition in the claim is that the Finality Sink must be positioned at or before the execution-finality boundary and must control whether the operation crosses that boundary. That positioning is significant. Consider: Authorization server → AI agent → application → OS → driver → NIC Checking authorization only near the beginning of this chain does not necessarily prove that the same operation eventually reached the NIC unchanged. The claim instead requires a structure effectively resembling: Authorization and protected state↓bound capability↓application↓OS/driver↓ Finality Sink ↓NIC transmission The Finality Sink effectively determines: “Is the exact operation about to be released the same operation that was authorized under the relevant protected state?” That is a more precise functional interpretation of Finality Sink than merely describing it as a policy enforcement point. 5. Machine-Verifiable Act Descriptor The machine-verifiable act descriptor answers: Exactly what operation is being authorized? For a SEND operation, it might represent: operation = SEND source = account-A object_digest = 75AE... destination = partner.example.com protocol = HTTPS purpose = regulatory-report maximum_bytes = 8MB expiry = T The actual encoding may use CBOR, JSON, Protocol Buffers, a canonical binary structure, a digest tree, or another deterministic representation. The important requirement is not the particular format. The important requirement is that the representation be deterministic enough for machines to compare what was authorized with what is actually about to happen. Conventional terminology includes: canonicalized request,transaction descriptor,command envelope,signed request parameters, oroperation manifest. 6. Authority Predicates A predicate is essentially a condition that evaluates to true or false. The claim refers to a: “set of machine-verifiable authority predicates” Such conditions may include: user_role == administrator AND operation == SEND AND destination == approved_destination AND file_classification 0 This corresponds to familiar concepts such as: RBAC conditions,ABAC predicates,policy rules,authorization constraints, orpolicy-decision logic. The wording is broader because authority does not necessarily have to originate from a conventional IAM system. 7. Protected Enforcement Domain The protected enforcement domain is a trusted or isolated environment in which security-critical validation occurs so that ordinary application code cannot freely manipulate the validation process or outcome. Claim 2 expressly provides examples such as: secure processor,trusted execution environment (TEE),hardware security module (HSM),secure element,programmable network interface,data-processing unit (DPU),protected controller, etc. Functionally: Protected Enforcement Domain ≈ isolated trusted computing environment containing critical reference-monitor or policy-enforcement logic. Possible implementations include: Intel TDX/SGX-like environmentsARM TrustZone-type environmentsHSMssmart NICs / DPUssecure elementsmicrocontroller protection domainsisolated hypervisor components The claim therefore does not depend upon one particular vendor implementation. 8. Protected-State Operation The architecture does not rely only on static credentials or static authorization. The protected domain may also read or modify security-sensitive mutable state. Examples include: revocation generationnonce stateanti-replay countersingle-use stateremaining quotacurrent policy versioncurrent authorization epochdevice operating state For example: capability_generation = 47 current_generation = 48 The older capability is invalid even if its cryptographic signature remains mathematically correct. Industry equivalents include: secure state lookup,trusted state transition,monotonic counter check,policy epoch check,anti-replay state update, etc. 9. Protected-State Representation The protected-state representation identifies: Which security state did the authorization decision depend upon? For example: epoch = 91 policy_version = 7 revocation_generation = 22 nonce_counter = 1433 quota_state = 4 The representation may alternatively be a cryptographic digest or protected reference identifying that state. The important property is that the authorization decision cannot later become detached from the state under which it was made. In conventional terminology: protected-state representation ≈ trusted state snapshot / state version / state digest / security epoch representation. 10. Protected Validation Evidence Protected validation evidence is evidence that: the relevant predicates were actually evaluated and they were evaluated against a particular protected state. For example: act_digest = H(ACT) policy_version = 7 epoch = 91 decision = ALLOW timestamp = T validation_digest = H(...) MAC/signature = ... Industry terminology may include: authorization decision record,tamper-evident audit evidence,signed validation result,attestation evidence, orcryptographically protected decision receipt. An important aspect of the claim is the ordering: evidence must be committed before, or atomically with, making the capability available. This resembles transactional ordering and commit semantics. It prevents a sequence such as: issue authorization first → maybe record evidence later from satisfying the claimed sequence. 11. Scoped Non-Bearer Capability The expression scoped non-bearer capability combines several established concepts. Capability A capability is an artifact representing permission to perform an operation. Scoped The capability cannot authorize arbitrary operations. For example: SEND X → B does not authorize: SEND Y → C Non-Bearer Simply possessing or copying the capability should not by itself be sufficient to exercise it. A conventional bearer token behaves conceptually like: “Whoever holds this token can use it.” The claim requires something closer to: “This artifact is usable only for this exact act, at this intended sink and boundary, under these specified conditions.” Closest existing terminology includes: proof-of-possession authorization,sender-constrained token,object capability,transaction-specific capability,bound authorization token. However, the claim binds significantly more execution context than is ordinarily implied merely by the phrase “sender-constrained token.” 12. What Is Bound into the Capability? The capability is bound to multiple elements. Candidate Act Meaning: not some other operation. Act Descriptor Meaning: not substituted parameters. Validation Evidence Meaning: tied to the actual protected validation decision. Protected State Meaning: tied to the security state against which authorization occurred. Execution-Finality Boundary Meaning: tied to the intended consequence boundary. Finality Sink Meaning: another enforcement point cannot necessarily exercise the capability. Freshness Meaning: the capability cannot simply remain usable indefinitely. Effectuation Scope Meaning: the capability authorizes only the specified class or range of consequences. In conventional cryptographic and security terminology, this may be described as: cryptographic parameter binding + context binding + channel/resource binding + transaction binding + freshness binding. 13. Capability-Validity Check At the Finality Sink, the system verifies the capability. Such verification may include: verify MAC/signature verify act digest verify sink identity verify boundary identity verify freshness verify nonce verify generation verify revocation state verify scope verify evidence digest verify protected-state reference verify not previously consumed Accordingly: machine-enforced capability-validity check ≈ final policy-enforcement or capability/token-validation procedure. The distinguishing architectural point is where the validation occurs: immediately before the controlled effect. 14. External Effectuation External effectuation means: the operation actually causes its intended side effect. It does not necessarily mean “external to the computer.” For these claims, the relevant effect may include: network transmissionpersistent storage commitmemory modificationDMA transactionaccelerator egressRF emissionoptical transmissionmotor movementpower switching Accordingly, a more conventional engineering description is: externally consequential or protected state-changing side effect. 15. Fail Closed Fail closed is established cybersecurity terminology. The architecture specifies that if an important authorization or verification condition cannot be established, the operation does not proceed. Conceptually: VALID → may effectuate INVALID → deny MISSING → deny STALE → deny REVOKED → deny REPLAYED → deny UNKNOWN → deny UNVERIFIABLE → deny TIMEOUT → deny This corresponds to: default deny / fail secure. It differs from architectures that permit execution when authorization infrastructure, current policy state, or relevant validation information is unavailable. 16. Exhausted Exhausted means that an authorization resource has already been consumed or has reached its permitted use limit. For example: Capability permits one SEND. SEND #1 → permitted Capability marked consumed. SEND #2 → exhausted → denied. Conventional terminology includes: single-use capability,spent authorization, orconsumed token. 17. Indeterminate An indeterminate state exists when the system cannot reliably establish whether authorization remains valid. For example: revocation database reachable? policy version correct? counter synchronized? authorization state valid? The claim treats: UNKNOWN differently from: VALID and therefore requires: UNKNOWN → no effectuation This corresponds closely to: indeterminate policy decision → deny. What Claim 2A Means Claim 2A identifies possible implementations of the Finality Sink for digital or computational side effects. For example: Network-interface controller / DPU / programmable NIC The enforcement point can stop bytes before they physically or logically leave the trusted machine or controlled environment. Memory-controller / memory-commit interface The enforcement point can stop a protected state change before the memory transaction commits. Storage-controller commit interface The enforcement point can prevent persistent data modification until the required authorization has been validated. DMA commit interface The enforcement point can prevent unauthorized direct-memory transfers. Accelerator egress interface The enforcement point can prevent GPU, NPU, or other AI-accelerator output from leaving the controlled computation domain. Accordingly, Claim 2A can be summarized functionally as: Place the reference monitor or enforcement gate at the actual digital side-effect interface. What Claim 2B Means Claim 2B applies the same architecture to the physical and control-system domain. For example: RF Transmit Interface The enforcement point controls whether radio-frequency energy is actually transmitted. Beamforming-Control Interface The enforcement point can prevent an antenna array from generating or emitting the commanded beam. Motor-Control Interface Software may calculate: MOVE MOTOR 30° but the motor does not move until the relevant enforcement point releases the command. Propulsion-Control Interface An AI or control system may determine: THRUST but generation of that computational decision does not itself constitute authority to physically produce thrust. This corresponds to safety and control-system concepts such as: command gating / actuation interlock / safety interlock at the physical output boundary. End-to-End Industry Example Consider a SEND operation: AI system proposes SEND File X to Destination B. Ordinary high-level authorization may resemble: AI → OAuth/IAM authorization → application → SEND The claimed architecture is more like: AI proposes SEND X→B ↓ Hold the SEND Nothing leaves yet. ↓ Create canonical transaction descriptor SEND file = X destination = B account = A purpose = P ↓ Trusted enforcement environment validates authority ↓ Trusted enforcement environment checks protected security state Examples include: revocation, epoch, nonce, quota, policy version, generation state, etc. ↓ Commit protected validation evidence For example: “This exact SEND was validated against protected state S.” ↓ Generate scoped non-bearer capability Bound to: SEND X→B evidence E state S sink F boundary Z freshness T scope P ↓ Finality Sink at NIC/DPU Egress The enforcement point reconstructs or checks what is actually about to leave. ↓ The actual operation is compared against the bound capability. ↓ If all required conditions correspond: Transmit If any required condition does not correspond: Do Not Transmit This expresses the architecture in conventional engineering terms while preserving the distinction between authorization upstream and enforcement at the actual consequence boundary. Most Important Architecture-Specific Terms and Industry Equivalents Claim terminology Best searchable conventional equivalents Candidate Act staged operation, transaction intent, pending command, prepared request Finality Sink reference monitor, policy enforcement point, commit gate, command gate, actuation gate, egress enforcement point Execution-finality boundary side-effect boundary, commit point, actuation boundary, egress boundary, irreversible-operation boundary Execution finality final side-effect authorization, transactional enforcement, consequence gating Non-effective hold state pre-commit state, staged state, prepared state, interlocked state Protected validation evidence signed authorization-decision record, tamper-evident decision evidence, attestation record Protected-state representation trusted state snapshot, state version, security epoch, protected-state digest Scoped non-bearer capability transaction-bound capability, proof-of-possession authorization, sender-constrained authorization artifact External effectuation side effect, commit, egress, actuation, externally observable state transition Permitted effectuation scope authorization scope, permitted transaction/action/resource constraints Central Rule in Conventional Industry Terminology A proposed side-effecting operation is staged rather than immediately executed; its exact parameters are canonicalized; authorization and mutable security state are checked within a protected enforcement environment; the resulting decision and state are integrity-protected; a transaction-specific, non-transferable authorization capability is created; and the reference monitor controlling the actual commit, egress, disclosure, or actuation independently verifies that capability against the exact operation immediately before releasing the side effect, with default-deny behavior on any mismatch, replay, revocation, expiry, or indeterminate state. This is a conventional engineering-language description of the functional architecture of Claims 1 and 2 without relying exclusively on the specialized labels Candidate Act, Finality Sink, or execution finality.

Finality Sink Strongly architecture-specific/coined policy enforcement point, reference monitor, command gate, actuation gate, commit gate, egress gate, safety interlock The component controlling the last practical point before the consequence occurs. machine-enforced capability-validity check Descriptive token verification, capability verification, PoP verification, authorization enforcement The Finality Sink independently checks that the authorization artifact is valid before releasing the operation. external effectuation Specialized side effect, output commit, egress, transmission, actuation, externally observable state transition The moment the proposed operation actually causes a consequence. fail closed Fully standard security term default deny, fail secure If verification fails or cannot be completed, the consequence is prevented. replayed Fully standard replay attack An earlier valid authorization or operation is reused. exhausted Somewhat specialized in this context consumed capability, spent nonce, used-once authorization, quota exhausted The authorization was single-use or limited-use and has already been consumed. indeterminate Standard policy/security concept decision unavailable, PDP indeterminate, unverifiable state The system cannot reliably determine whether authorization is valid. The claim requires denial rather than guessing. 1. Candidate Act A Candidate Act is: A fully or sufficiently specified operation that the system intends to perform, but which has not yet been permitted to create its actual consequence. Suppose an AI agent determines that a file should be sent: SEND file financial-report.pdf to partner.example.com An ordinary system may operate approximately as follows: AI decision → API call → network stack → SEND Under the architecture: AI decision→ construct SEND(file_hash=X, destination=partner.example.com, protocol=HTTPS, account=A...) → hold that exact operation as the Candidate Act The operation can therefore be inspected, validated, and bound to authorization before packets actually leave the controlled boundary. In conventional terminology: Candidate Act ≈ staged command / pending transaction / transaction intent / prepared operation. The usefulness of the terminology is that a conventional word such as “request” can sometimes refer to something already transmitted or submitted. Candidate Act expressly identifies a state in which: the operation exists, but its consequence does not yet exist. 2. Non-Effective Hold State The non-effective hold state is the state in which the Candidate Act remains before release. It means: The operation has been computed or prepared, but some mechanism prevents it from yet producing the protected consequence. This resembles the prepare stage in transactional systems. For example: Database UPDATE balance ... The update may have been constructed but is not yet committed. Network A message may have been constructed in memory but not yet transmitted through the NIC. Robot MOVE_ARM(x=20,y=15) The command may have been generated, but the motor-control signal remains inhibited. Accordingly: non-effective hold state ≈ staged / prepared / pre-commit / interlocked state. 3. Execution-Finality Boundary The execution-finality boundary identifies the point separating: something the computer intends to do from something that has actually become consequential. The specific boundary varies by technology. Domain Possible execution-finality boundary Network NIC/DPU transmission or egress Storage persistent write or commit Memory protected memory commit GPU/NPU accelerator output or egress Payment ledger or value-transfer commit Telecom RF transmission Satellite command or actuator interface Robot motor or actuator controller Power system switching or enable interface Data disclosure interface that actually releases protected bytes In conventional systems literature, this may be called the: side-effect boundary, commit point, actuation boundary, egress boundary, or irreversible-operation boundary. The claim generalizes those domain-specific boundaries under a common architectural concept. 4. Finality Sink The Finality Sink is not simply another authorization server. It is the enforcement component controlling the actual consequence. In ordinary industry terminology, depending on the implementation, it may correspond functionally to a: reference monitorpolicy enforcement point (PEP)command gateactuation gatetransaction commit gateegress enforcement pointsafety interlock An important additional condition in the claim is that the Finality Sink must be positioned at or before the execution-finality boundary and must control whether the operation crosses that boundary. That positioning is significant. Consider: Authorization server → AI agent → application → OS → driver → NIC Checking authorization only near the beginning of this chain does not necessarily prove that the same operation eventually reached the NIC unchanged. The claim instead requires a structure effectively resembling: Authorization and protected state↓bound capability↓application↓OS/driver↓ Finality Sink ↓NIC transmission The Finality Sink effectively determines: “Is the exact operation about to be released the same operation that was authorized under the relevant protected state?” That is a more precise functional interpretation of Finality Sink than merely describing it as a policy enforcement point. 5. Machine-Verifiable Act Descriptor The machine-verifiable act descriptor answers: Exactly what operation is being authorized? For a SEND operation, it might represent: operation = SEND source = account-A object_digest = 75AE... destination = partner.example.com protocol = HTTPS purpose = regulatory-report maximum_bytes = 8MB expiry = T The actual encoding may use CBOR, JSON, Protocol Buffers, a canonical binary structure, a digest tree, or another deterministic representation. The important requirement is not the particular format. The important requirement is that the representation be deterministic enough for machines to compare what was authorized with what is actually about to happen. Conventional terminology includes: canonicalized request,transaction descriptor,command envelope,signed request parameters, oroperation manifest. 6. Authority Predicates A predicate is essentially a condition that evaluates to true or false. The claim refers to a: “set of machine-verifiable authority predicates” Such conditions may include: user_role == administrator AND operation == SEND AND destination == approved_destination AND file_classification 0 This corresponds to familiar concepts such as: RBAC conditions,ABAC predicates,policy rules,authorization constraints, orpolicy-decision logic. The wording is broader because authority does not necessarily have to originate from a conventional IAM system. 7. Protected Enforcement Domain The protected enforcement domain is a trusted or isolated environment in which security-critical validation occurs so that ordinary application code cannot freely manipulate the validation process or outcome. Claim 2 expressly provides examples such as: secure processor,trusted execution environment (TEE),hardware security module (HSM),secure element,programmable network interface,data-processing unit (DPU),protected controller, etc. Functionally: Protected Enforcement Domain ≈ isolated trusted computing environment containing critical reference-monitor or policy-enforcement logic. Possible implementations include: Intel TDX/SGX-like environmentsARM TrustZone-type environmentsHSMssmart NICs / DPUssecure elementsmicrocontroller protection domainsisolated hypervisor components The claim therefore does not depend upon one particular vendor implementation. 8. Protected-State Operation The architecture does not rely only on static credentials or static authorization. The protected domain may also read or modify security-sensitive mutable state. Examples include: revocation generationnonce stateanti-replay countersingle-use stateremaining quotacurrent policy versioncurrent authorization epochdevice operating state For example: capability_generation = 47 current_generation = 48 The older capability is invalid even if its cryptographic signature remains mathematically correct. Industry equivalents include: secure state lookup,trusted state transition,monotonic counter check,policy epoch check,anti-replay state update, etc. 9. Protected-State Representation The protected-state representation identifies: Which security state did the authorization decision depend upon? For example: epoch = 91 policy_version = 7 revocation_generation = 22 nonce_counter = 1433 quota_state = 4 The representation may alternatively be a cryptographic digest or protected reference identifying that state. The important property is that the authorization decision cannot later become detached from the state under which it was made. In conventional terminology: protected-state representation ≈ trusted state snapshot / state version / state digest / security epoch representation. 10. Protected Validation Evidence Protected validation evidence is evidence that: the relevant predicates were actually evaluated and they were evaluated against a particular protected state. For example: act_digest = H(ACT) policy_version = 7 epoch = 91 decision = ALLOW timestamp = T validation_digest = H(...) MAC/signature = ... Industry terminology may include: authorization decision record,tamper-evident audit evidence,signed validation result,attestation evidence, orcryptographically protected decision receipt. An important aspect of the claim is the ordering: evidence must be committed before, or atomically with, making the capability available. This resembles transactional ordering and commit semantics. It prevents a sequence such as: issue authorization first → maybe record evidence later from satisfying the claimed sequence. 11. Scoped Non-Bearer Capability The expression scoped non-bearer capability combines several established concepts. Capability A capability is an artifact representing permission to perform an operation. Scoped The capability cannot authorize arbitrary operations. For example: SEND X → B does not authorize: SEND Y → C Non-Bearer Simply possessing or copying the capability should not by itself be sufficient to exercise it. A conventional bearer token behaves conceptually like: “Whoever holds this token can use it.” The claim requires something closer to: “This artifact is usable only for this exact act, at this intended sink and boundary, under these specified conditions.” Closest existing terminology includes: proof-of-possession authorization,sender-constrained token,object capability,transaction-specific capability,bound authorization token. However, the claim binds significantly more execution context than is ordinarily implied merely by the phrase “sender-constrained token.” 12. What Is Bound into the Capability? The capability is bound to multiple elements. Candidate Act Meaning: not some other operation. Act Descriptor Meaning: not substituted parameters. Validation Evidence Meaning: tied to the actual protected validation decision. Protected State Meaning: tied to the security state against which authorization occurred. Execution-Finality Boundary Meaning: tied to the intended consequence boundary. Finality Sink Meaning: another enforcement point cannot necessarily exercise the capability. Freshness Meaning: the capability cannot simply remain usable indefinitely. Effectuation Scope Meaning: the capability authorizes only the specified class or range of consequences. In conventional cryptographic and security terminology, this may be described as: cryptographic parameter binding + context binding + channel/resource binding + transaction binding + freshness binding. 13. Capability-Validity Check At the Finality Sink, the system verifies the capability. Such verification may include: verify MAC/signature verify act digest verify sink identity verify boundary identity verify freshness verify nonce verify generation verify revocation state verify scope verify evidence digest verify protected-state reference verify not previously consumed Accordingly: machine-enforced capability-validity check ≈ final policy-enforcement or capability/token-validation procedure. The distinguishing architectural point is where the validation occurs: immediately before the controlled effect. 14. External Effectuation External effectuation means: the operation actually causes its intended side effect. It does not necessarily mean “external to the computer.” For these claims, the relevant effect may include: network transmissionpersistent storage commitmemory modificationDMA transactionaccelerator egressRF emissionoptical transmissionmotor movementpower switching Accordingly, a more conventional engineering description is: externally consequential or protected state-changing side effect. 15. Fail Closed Fail closed is established cybersecurity terminology. The architecture specifies that if an important authorization or verification condition cannot be established, the operation does not proceed. Conceptually: VALID → may effectuate INVALID → deny MISSING → deny STALE → deny REVOKED → deny REPLAYED → deny UNKNOWN → deny UNVERIFIABLE → deny TIMEOUT → deny This corresponds to: default deny / fail secure. It differs from architectures that permit execution when authorization infrastructure, current policy state, or relevant validation information is unavailable. 16. Exhausted Exhausted means that an authorization resource has already been consumed or has reached its permitted use limit. For example: Capability permits one SEND. SEND #1 → permitted Capability marked consumed. SEND #2 → exhausted → denied. Conventional terminology includes: single-use capability,spent authorization, orconsumed token. 17. Indeterminate An indeterminate state exists when the system cannot reliably establish whether authorization remains valid. For example: revocation database reachable? policy version correct? counter synchronized? authorization state valid? The claim treats: UNKNOWN differently from: VALID and therefore requires: UNKNOWN → no effectuation This corresponds closely to: indeterminate policy decision → deny. What Claim 2A Means Claim 2A identifies possible implementations of the Finality Sink for digital or computational side effects. For example: Network-interface controller / DPU / programmable NIC The enforcement point can stop bytes before they physically or logically leave the trusted machine or controlled environment. Memory-controller / memory-commit interface The enforcement point can stop a protected state change before the memory transaction commits. Storage-controller commit interface The enforcement point can prevent persistent data modification until the required authorization has been validated. DMA commit interface The enforcement point can prevent unauthorized direct-memory transfers. Accelerator egress interface The enforcement point can prevent GPU, NPU, or other AI-accelerator output from leaving the controlled computation domain. Accordingly, Claim 2A can be summarized functionally as: Place the reference monitor or enforcement gate at the actual digital side-effect interface. What Claim 2B Means Claim 2B applies the same architecture to the physical and control-system domain. For example: RF Transmit Interface The enforcement point controls whether radio-frequency energy is actually transmitted. Beamforming-Control Interface The enforcement point can prevent an antenna array from generating or emitting the commanded beam. Motor-Control Interface Software may calculate: MOVE MOTOR 30° but the motor does not move until the relevant enforcement point releases the command. Propulsion-Control Interface An AI or control system may determine: THRUST but generation of that computational decision does not itself constitute authority to physically produce thrust. This corresponds to safety and control-system concepts such as: command gating / actuation interlock / safety interlock at the physical output boundary. End-to-End Industry Example Consider a SEND operation: AI system proposes SEND File X to Destination B. Ordinary high-level authorization may resemble: AI → OAuth/IAM authorization → application → SEND The claimed architecture is more like: AI proposes SEND X→B ↓ Hold the SEND Nothing leaves yet. ↓ Create canonical transaction descriptor SEND file = X destination = B account = A purpose = P ↓ Trusted enforcement environment validates authority ↓ Trusted enforcement environment checks protected security state Examples include: revocation, epoch, nonce, quota, policy version, generation state, etc. ↓ Commit protected validation evidence For example: “This exact SEND was validated against protected state S.” ↓ Generate scoped non-bearer capability Bound to: SEND X→B evidence E state S sink F boundary Z freshness T scope P ↓ Finality Sink at NIC/DPU Egress The enforcement point reconstructs or checks what is actually about to leave. ↓ The actual operation is compared against the bound capability. ↓ If all required conditions correspond: Transmit If any required condition does not correspond: Do Not Transmit This expresses the architecture in conventional engineering terms while preserving the distinction between authorization upstream and enforcement at the actual consequence boundary. Most Important Architecture-Specific Terms and Industry Equivalents Claim terminology Best searchable conventional equivalents Candidate Act staged operation, transaction intent, pending command, prepared request Finality Sink reference monitor, policy enforcement point, commit gate, command gate, actuation gate, egress enforcement point Execution-finality boundary side-effect boundary, commit point, actuation boundary, egress boundary, irreversible-operation boundary Execution finality final side-effect authorization, transactional enforcement, consequence gating Non-effective hold state pre-commit state, staged state, prepared state, interlocked state Protected validation evidence signed authorization-decision record, tamper-evident decision evidence, attestation record Protected-state representation trusted state snapshot, state version, security epoch, protected-state digest Scoped non-bearer capability transaction-bound capability, proof-of-possession authorization, sender-constrained authorization artifact External effectuation side effect, commit, egress, actuation, externally observable state transition Permitted effectuation scope authorization scope, permitted transaction/action/resource constraints Central Rule in Conventional Industry Terminology A proposed side-effecting operation is staged rather than immediately executed; its exact parameters are canonicalized; authorization and mutable security state are checked within a protected enforcement environment; the resulting decision and state are integrity-protected; a transaction-specific, non-transferable authorization capability is created; and the reference monitor controlling the actual commit, egress, disclosure, or actuation independently verifies that capability against the exact operation immediately before releasing the side effect, with default-deny behavior on any mismatch, replay, revocation, expiry, or indeterminate state. This is a conventional engineering-language description of the functional architecture of Claims 1 and 2 without relying exclusively on the specialized labels Candidate Act, Finality Sink, or execution finality.

candidates.title: IMD: A 6-DoF Pose Estimation Benchmark for Industrial Metallic Objects
candidates.description: Object 6DoF (6D) pose estimation is essential for robotic perception, especially in industrial settings. It enables robots to interact with the environment and manipulate objects. However, existing benchmarks on object 6D pose estimation primarily use everyday objects with rich textures and low-reflectivity, limiting model generalization to industrial scenarios where objects are often metallic, texture-less, and highly reflective. To address this gap, we propose a novel dataset and benchmark namely Industrial Metallic Dataset (IMD), tailored for industrial applications. Our dataset comprises 45 true-to-scale industrial components, captured with an RGB-D camera under natural indoor lighting and varied object arrangements to replicate real-world conditions. The benchmark supports three tasks, including video object segmentation, 6D pose tracking, and one-shot 6D pose estimation. We evaluate existing state-of-the-art models, including XMem and SAM2 for segmentation, and BundleTrack and BundleSDF for pose estimation, to assess model performance in industrial contexts. Evaluation results show that our industrial dataset is more challenging than existing household object datasets. This benchmark provides the baseline for developing and comparing segmentation and pose estimation algorithms that better generalize to industrial robotics scenarios.

candidates.title: High-resolution deformation mapping of martensitic transformation and plasticity in superelastic Nickel-Titanium
candidates.description: Shape-memory alloys (SMAs) such as nitinol (NiTi) can recover large strains through a reversible stress- or temperature-induced martensitic transformation, but cyclic transformation degrades reversibility. Recent experimental evidence has linked this functional fatigue to the emission of dislocations from the fine martensitic microstructure that forms near the phase boundary, but the precise coupling mechanism between dislocation slip and martensitic microstructure is still widely debated. This creates a mesoscale gap in the understanding of SMAs and their fatigue: multiscale simulation is prohibitively expensive, while experimental methods that can spatially resolve fine microstructure and individual dislocations (e.g., transmission electron microscopy) cannot capture bulk mechanical behavior. In biomedical applications, understanding and modeling the mechanisms of slip localization and functional fatigue will be particularly crucial for the newest generations of ultra-high-purity nitinol, with flaw sizes below the theoretical crack length threshold. In the work to which this dataset is linked, we develop a new framework (MMICROSTRUCTURE) to reconstruct the geometrically necessary martensitic transformation and plastic slip in polycrystalline SMAs from high-resolution, full-field deformation maps. Using digital image correlation in a scanning electron microscope (SEM-DIC), we experimentally measure deformation with approximately 200 nanometer spatial resolution over a 0.5-millimeter field of view. We align this deformation data to austenite grain structure mapped via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Using the MMICROSTRUCTURE framework, we quantitatively map the activity of individual slip systems and martensitic variants in each DIC subset. We show that localized networks of coupled slip and martensitic reorientation form microstructural "bridges" that propagate transformation through clusters of poorly oriented grains. The energy dissipated during bridging may be the origin of the unusual prestrain effects in nitinol, where higher prestrains (for example, crimping of a medical device) have been correlated to increased fatigue strength. Contrary to recent theories of functional fatigue focusing on a Type II twin interface, we observe that the most intense slip localization events are coupled to the development of Type I twins with a finite width.

candidates.title: Supplemental data from: Inference of phylogenetic networks from sequence data using composite likelihood
candidates.description: While phylogenies have been essential in understanding how species evolve, they do not adequately describe some evolutionary processes. For instance, hybridization, a common phenomenon where interbreeding between two species leads to the formation of a new species, must be depicted by a phylogenetic network, a structure that modifies a phylogenetic tree by allowing two branches to merge into one, resulting in reticulation. However, existing methods for estimating networks become computationally expensive as the dataset size and/or topological complexity increase. The lack of methods for scalable inference hampers phylogenetic networks from being widely used in practice, despite accumulating evidence that hybridization occurs frequently in nature. Here, we propose a novel method, PhyNEST (Phylogenetic Network Estimation using SiTe patterns), that estimates binary, level-1 phylogenetic networks with a fixed, user-specified number of reticulations directly from sequence data. By using the composite likelihood as the basis for inference, PhyNEST is able to use the full genomic data in a computationally tractable manner, eliminating the need to summarize the data as a set of gene trees prior to network estimation. To search network space, PhyNEST implements both hill climbing and simulated annealing algorithms. PhyNEST assumes that the data are composed of coalescent independent sites that evolve according to the Jukes-Cantor substitution model and that the network has a constant effective population size. Simulation studies demonstrate that PhyNEST is often more accurate than two existing composite likelihood summary methods (SNaQ and PhyloNet) and that it is robust to at least one form of model misspecification (assuming a less complex nucleotide substitution model than the true generating model). We applied PhyNEST to reconstruct the evolutionary relationships among Heliconius butterflies and Papionini primates, characterized by hybrid speciation and widespread introgression, respectively. PhyNEST is implemented in an open-source Julia package and is publicly available at https://github.com/sungsik-kong/PhyNEST.jl.

candidates.title: AI ROI Dataset: 200 B2B Deployments Analysis (2022-2025)
candidates.description: This dataset presents an empirical analysis of 200 artificial intelligence (AI) deployments in French B2B companies between 2022 and 2025. Using structured data collection methods including CRM exports, quarterly interviews, and financial audits, we document median ROI of +347% in Year 1, with an 8-month breakeven period and a 27% failure rate. Key Findings: - 200 AI projects across 10 business sectors - Median ROI: +347% in Year 1 - Success rate: 82.5% (vs. 5-20% market average) - Average breakeven: 8 months - Small budgets ( €100K) - Human-in-the-Loop governance reduces critical incidents by 4.3× Dataset Structure: 20 variables including project_id, year, quarter, sector, company_size, revenue, ai_use_case, deployment_type, investment, annual_gain, roi_percent, time_saved, failure status, and human-in-the-loop adoption. Related DOI: - Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17795133 - Figshare: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.30795017 Author ORCID: 0009-0007-0785-7305

candidates.title: Multi-Topic Reddit Political User Interactions
candidates.description: The data comes from a selection of political subreddits for the 2007-2022 period. For each week in this period we have user networks. The nodes are Reddit users, connected by an undirected edge if they have exchanged a statistically significant number of messages. For each user we have a stance value which is their average opinion on that week for seven political topics of interest: abortion, climate, gender, guns, health, unauthorized immigration, and racial issues. We also have a PCA value reducing the 7-dimensional stance to their main component. Finally, we also have the network community to which the user belongs. For each edge we have the following attributes: the weight (number of messages the two users exchanged in that week), a significance score (the higher the more significant the message), the average level of toxicity of the messages the two users exchanged, and the disagreement between the users (the absolute value of the difference of their PCA scores). Additionally, we have a database with all Reddit messages in our study. It is a single tab-separated file with the following columns: user id of the author of the message the detected topic of the message (using BERTopic) the toxicity of the message (using detoxify) the stance of the message on the topic (using Llama 3) the week in which the message was sent the subreddit in which the message was sent the rolling opinion of the user (averaging the last 4 messages the user sent on that topic) the weekly opinion of the user (averaging all messages the user sent on that topic in that week, even if they are more than 4) Note that the user ids in the networks and in the message database are not consistent. This is because the networks are preprocessed to be quickly loaded in torch_geometric, which require reindexing so that nodes have ids between 0 and n-1, without gaps. To use this dataset, we refer to our Github repository: https://github.com/mikk-c/mdim_polarization/

candidates.title: DECMA-1 main data set for: Shape-independent fluidity in epithelial cell monolayers
candidates.description: This repository contains an integrated dataset of time-lapse fluorescence microscopy and laser ablation experiments designed to investigate how reduced E-cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion regulates the collective dynamics and mechanical properties of epithelial monolayers. Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) epithelial cells expressing nuclear-localized GFP (MDCK NLS) were cultured as approximately 1 mm diameter islands on 6 kPa polyacrylamide substrates. Cell proliferation was inhibited using mitomycin C to maintain a nearly constant cell density throughout the experiments, enabling the effects of adhesion perturbation to be isolated from density-dependent changes. The experiments were performed in parallel under identical biological conditions using five DECMA-1 treatment groups: a sham control (0 μg ml -1 ) and four concentrations of the E-cadherin blocking antibody DECMA-1 (2.5, 5.0, 7.5, and 10.0 μg ml -1 ). Time-series imaging was carried out on substrates containing embedded fluorescent beads to quantify collective cell migration, cell morphology, and cell-substrate traction forces. In parallel, laser ablation experiments were performed on matched cultures without embedded beads to quantify cell-cell junction mechanics through post-ablation junction retraction dynamics. The time-series dataset consists of 24-hour fluorescence image sequences acquired every 15 minutes (97 time points per field of view), including nuclear, cell-body, bead, and reference-bead image stacks. The laser ablation dataset consists of high-speed image sequences acquired at 1-second intervals following approximately 50 junction ablations for each treatment condition. Together, these complementary datasets provide measurements of collective migration, traction forces, cell morphology, structural relaxation, and junctional tension across a controlled range of E-cadherin inhibition. The data were generated using an established MDCK cell line and contain no human participant data, personally identifiable information, or animal subjects. Users are requested to cite the associated publication when using these data.

candidates.title: Sequential human assembly and disassembly motions in human-robot coexisting environments
candidates.description: As human-robot systems and autonomous robots become increasingly prevalent, the need for task-oriented datasets to study human behaviors in shared spaces has grown significantly. We present a novel dataset focusing on sequential human assembly and disassembly motions in human-robot coexisting environments. It contains over 10,000 samples recorded from multi-view camera setups, each comprising synchronized RGB videos and 2D and 3D human skeletons. Data were collected from 33 participants with diverse physical characteristics and behavior preferences. This dataset highlights practical challenges such as partial occlusions, similar repetitive motions, and varying human behaviors, which are often overlooked in existing datasets and research. Technical validation using benchmarking with state-of-the-art deep learning models reveals significant potential in using this dataset for practical applications. To support diverse research applications, this dataset provides raw and processed data with detailed annotations, including precise timestamps, procedure annotations, and Python codes for reproducibility. It aims to advance research in human motion prediction, task-oriented robotic sequential decision-making, motion and task planning of autonomous robots, and human-robot collaborative policies.

candidates.title: It Takes a Village to Build a Robot: An Empirical Study of The ROS Ecosystem - Replication Package
candidates.description: Over the past eleven years, the Robot Operating System (ROS), has grown from a small research project into the most popular framework for robotics development. Composed of packages released on the Rosdistro package manager, ROS aims to simplify development by providing reusable libraries, tools and conventions for building a robot. Still, developing a complete robot is a difficult task that involves bridging many technical disciplines. Experts who create computer vision packages, for instance, may need to rely on software designed by mechanical engineers to implement motor control. As building a robot requires domain expertise in software, mechanical, and electrical engineering, as well as artificial intelligence and robotics, ROS faces knowledge based barriers to collaboration. In this paper, we examine how the necessity of domain specific knowledge impacts the open source collaboration model. We create a comprehensive corpus of package metadata and dependencies over three years in the ROS ecosystem, analyze how collaboration is structured, and study the dependency network evolution. We find that the most widely used ROS packages belong to a small cluster of foundational working groups (FWGs), each organized around a different domain in robotics. We show that the FWGs are growing at a slower rate than the rest of the ecosystem, in terms of their membership and number of packages, yet the number of dependencies on FWGs is increasing at a faster rate. In addition, we mined all ROS packages on GitHub, and showed that 82% rely exclusively on functionality provided by FWGs. Finally, we investigate these highly influential groups and describe the unique model of collaboration they support in ROS.

candidates.title: Objectifying the Subjective: Cognitive Biases in Topic Interpretations
candidates.description: Abstract: Interpretation of topics is crucial for their downstream applications. State-of-the-art evaluation measures of topic quality such as coherence and word intrusion do not measure how much a topic facilitates the exploration of a corpus. To design evaluation measures grounded on a task, and a population of users, we do user studies to understand how users interpret topics. We propose constructs of topic quality and ask users to assess them in the context of a topic and provide rationale behind evaluations. We use reflexive thematic analysis to identify themes of topic interpretations from rationales. Users interpret topics based on availability and representativeness heuristics rather than probability. We propose a theory of topic interpretation based on the anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic: users anchor on salient words and make semantic adjustments to arrive at an interpretation. Topic interpretation can be viewed as making a judgment under uncertainty by an ecologically rational user, and hence cognitive biases aware user models and evaluation frameworks are needed. Datasets: Our first dataset is ACL OCL by (Rohatgi et al., 2023) ( ACL ) a scholarly corpus of papers hosted by the ACL Anthology published from 1952 to September 2022. As a second dataset, we consider U.S. Senate Speeches ( SENATE ), the texts of U.S. Senate speeches provided by (Gentzkow et al., 2019). We focus on the speeches in the 114th session of Congress (2015-2017). The third dataset consists of ``Software Design'' ( DESIGN ) related posts on StackOverflow (SO). Each SO post is allowed to have up to 5 tags that assigns the topic of the post. (Mahadi et al., 2020) use 10 software-design related SO tags (viz. “design-patterns”, “software-design”, “class-design”, “design-principles”, “system-design”, “code-design”, “api-design”, “language-design”, “dependency-injection” and “architecture”) to identify design-related posts on SO. We use SO API to extend the tags by querying tag descriptions (identified by PostTypes: TagWikiExcerpt and TagWiki) for the keyword “design” and having more than 100 posts. We manually removed tags that were not related to software design-related posts resulting in a set of 61 tags. We excluded UI design related tags such as css. We identified over 227 thousand design-related question-answer(s) pairs published till the end of December 2020 using the SOTorrent dataset (Baltes et al., 2019). (Datasets.zip contains the three datasets.) Preprocessing: We tokenized texts using the Spacy library with model ``en_core_web_sm'' . We discarded documents with less than five words. We used (Hoyel et al., 2021)'s library to do the pre-processing. Following (Vafa et al., 2020), we considered all the unigrams appearing in at least 0.1% and at most 30% of documents in the corpus. After pre-processing, the SENATE dataset had 17,573, the DESGIN dataset had 174,416 and the ACL dataset had 71,736 documents. User Interface: We customized the Potato text annotation tool by ( Pei et al., 2022 ) as an interface for the annotation task. (UserInterface.zip contains our customization of Potato) Annotations: (Annotations.zip contains user annotations of topics specific to each dataset.)

It provides the observations used to calculate Table I of the MCTA-Tracker manuscript. Four tracking methods were evaluated in five environments: Box, Wall, Maze, Forest, and Cave. Each row reports seven metrics describing target visibility, mean tracking distance, variation in tracking distance, cumulative tracking failure time, the minimum number of robots simultaneously tracking the target, and the mean and minimum angular coverage around the target. The accompanying Python script computes the mean and sample standard deviation for each group and reproduces the pairwise permutation tests with Holm correction. The README defines each column and explains how to interpret the reported values.InstructionsDownload table1_runs.csv and reproduce_table1.py and save both files in the same folder. Open a terminal in that folder and run the following command with Python 3.8 or later:python reproduce_table1.pyThe script uses only the Python standard library. It writes three files in the results folder. table1_summary.csv contains the group means, sample standard deviations, and Table I formatting indicators. table1_tests.csv contains the raw and Holm-adjusted p-values for the 105 comparisons. failure_duration_ranges.csv contains the minimum, median, and maximum cumulative tracking failure durations. See README.md for column definitions, units, and statistical conventions.Keywordsmulti-UAV tracking, target visibility, aerial robotics, simulation benchmarks

candidates.description: Thai SDG-labelled Text Corpus (v1.2) The Thai SDG-labelled Text Corpus is a publicly available dataset for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) text classification in Thai. The corpus contains 6,800 records evenly balanced across all 17 SDGs (400 records per goal). It was derived from the OSDG Community Dataset (OSDG-CD), Version 2024.04 (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11441197), translated into Thai using machine translation, with additional expert review of records flagged by automatic quality-control checks, and augmented with expert-reviewed synthetic data for SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals), which is not included in the original OSDG-CD. The dataset is intended to support Thai-language and multilingual natural language processing (NLP) research, including SDG classification, cross-lingual learning, information retrieval, and policy document analysis. Version 1.1 update Version 1.1 : Updated the dataset documentation and metadata to correct the author surname and update the source OSDG-CD citation to Version 2024.04 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11441197). Corrected the description of expert_agreement_score and the reporting of inter-annotator agreement. The field represents raw percent (observed) agreement and is not Cohen's kappa. A separately computed, chance-corrected Cohen's kappa is now reported alongside the original percent-agreement figures (pooled κ = 0.751; Expert_Verified_Pass κ = 0.847; Expert_Reviewed_Acceptable κ = 0.590; Expert_Flagged_Minor_Nuance κ = 0.537). Added Raw_Rater.xlsx, containing the raw Pass/Fail ratings from both human experts for 1,360 records × 20 rubric items, with the rubric provided bilingually in Thai and English. Added thai_sdg_cohens_kappa_en.xlsx, containing the complete Cohen's kappa calculations supporting the reported results, including row-level, verdict-subgroup, and per-criterion analyses. The underlying corpus files (thai_sdg_corpus_v1_0.csv and .xlsx) are unchanged. Version 1.1 consists of documentation and metadata corrections and the addition of supporting rater and kappa calculation files. Version 1.2 update Version 1.2: Updated the dataset documentation, metadata, and supporting materials to align with the revised manuscript and reviewer-requested reproducibility materials. The release adds Raw_RaterA.csv and Raw_RaterB.csv as separate raw rating files and retains the supporting files introduced in Version 1.1, including Raw_Rater.xlsx and thai_sdg_cohens_kappa_en.xlsx. It also includes the complete 20-item expert quality-assessment checklist and the prompt templates used for English-to-Thai translation, SDG 17 generation, and Thai-to-English back-translation. The SDG 1–16 translation and targeted expert-review workflow, SDG 17 provenance and distributional caveats, and the internal nature of the LaBSE threshold calibration are documented. The underlying corpus files (thai_sdg_corpus_v1_0.csv and .xlsx) remain unchanged. Version 1.2 consists of documentation, metadata, and supporting-file updates. Dataset Construction Records for SDG 1–16 were translated from English into Thai using machine translation, with additional expert review of records flagged by automatic quality-control checks, while SDG 17 records were newly generated and reviewed by experts. Each record includes automatic quality-control indicators based on LaBSE semantic similarity and length-ratio checks. A stratified sample of 1,360 records (80 per SDG) additionally includes human-expert quality assessments and inter-annotator agreement scores. candidates.title: Data from: Physically interpretable surrogate modeling of thermal fields in electronics cooling using combined proper orthogonal decomposition and neural networks
candidates.description: As advances in semiconductor technology drive higher power densities, thermal management is becoming increasingly crucial to maintaining the performance and reliability of devices. In recent decades, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has been widely used for thermal management system design. However, the computational requirement of CFD limits its use for comprehensive system optimization and digital twin active control systems, which require quick, high-fidelity thermal field prediction. Data-driven surrogate models address the speed limitations of CFD but are often treated as black boxes whose predictions are physically uninterpretable. Neural networks (NN) combined with proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) maintain the speedup of other surrogate models while offering a physically interpretable latent space. The interpretability of POD-NN learned representations remains largely unexplored. This work develops and demonstrates a POD-NN surrogate model framework to predict 2D thermal fields for a liquid-cooled dual-chip cold plate with four retained POD modes. The resultant model predicts fields 412,500 faster than CFD. An error decomposition analysis is used to assess the contribution of POD-based and NN-based error across a range of dataset sizes and identify an error floor dependent on the number of modes retained rather than dataset size. A systematic Pearson correlation analysis is used to link all four POD coefficients to identifiable physical features, and thermal resistance is mapped in latent space. The presented framework enables sensitivity analysis, design optimization, and active thermal control within the physics-aware POD coefficient space, and advances POD-NN architectures from accelerators to interpretable engineering design tools.

candidates.title: Data from: Secure and secret cooperation in robot swarms
candidates.description: The importance of swarm robotics systems in both academic research and real-world applications is steadily increasing. However, to reach widespread adoption, new models that ensure the secure cooperation of large groups of robots need to be developed. This work introduces a method to encapsulate cooperative robotic missions in an authenticated data structure known as Merkle tree. With this method, operators can provide the "blueprint" of the swarm's mission without disclosing its raw data. In other words, data verification can be separated from data itself. We propose a system where robots in a swarm, to cooperate towards mission completion, have to "prove'' their integrity to their peers by exchanging cryptographic proofs. We show the implications of this approach for two different swarm robotics missions: foraging and maze formation. In both missions, swarm robots were able to cooperate and carry out sequential tasks without having explicit knowledge about the mission's high-level objectives. The results presented in this work demonstrate the feasibility of using Merkle trees as a cooperation mechanism for swarm robotics systems in both simulation and real-robot experiments, which has implications for future decentralized robotics applications where security plays a crucial role. This dataset includes all experimental data generated for this paper.

candidates.title: Global 0.25° daily observed and counterfactual fire weather index (1979–2024)
candidates.description: This is the associated dataset and code for the paper "Increasing Synchronicity of Global Extreme Fire Weather." To identify synchronous fire weather, we calculate daily Fire Weather Index (FWI) at 0.25° resolution for the period 1979–2024 using fifth-generation European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Reanalysis (ERA5) data, based on daily maximum air temperature, daily minimum relative humidity, daily mean wind speed, and daily total precipitation. We also apply an overwintering procedure in our calculations that accounts for inter-seasonal drought in cold climates. To assess the contribution of anthropogenic climate change, we apply the same methodology to derive counterfactual FWI that removes the first-order influence of modeled climate change in the variables used to calculate FWI. The counterfactual is constructed by subtracting the low-pass filtered signal of monthly changes in temperature, humidity, wind speed, and precipitation relative to a quasi-preindustrial climate (1850–1900) as simulated by the multi-model mean of 20 models participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) from the observational record.

candidates.title: Human activities with videos, inertial units and ambient sensors
candidates.description: Worldwide demographic projections point to a progressively older population. This fact has fostered research on Ambient Assisted Living, which includes developments on smart homes and social robots. To endow such environments with truly autonomous behaviours, algorithms must extract semantically meaningful information from whichever sensor data is available. Human activity recognition is one of the most active fields of research within this context. Proposed approaches vary according to the input modality and the environments considered. Different from others, this paper addresses the problem of recognising heterogeneous activities of daily living centred in home environments considering simultaneously data from videos, wearable IMUs and ambient sensors. For this, two contributions are presented. The first is the creation of the Heriot-Watt University/University of Sao Paulo (HWU-USP) activities dataset, which was recorded at the Robotic Assisted Living Testbed at Heriot-Watt University. This dataset differs from other multimodal datasets due to the fact that it consists of daily living activities with either periodical patterns or long-term dependencies, which are captured in a very rich and heterogeneous sensing environment. In particular, this dataset combines data from a humanoid robot’s RGBD (RGB + depth) camera, with inertial sensors from wearable devices, and ambient sensors from a smart home. The second contribution is the proposal of a Deep Learning (DL) framework, which provides multimodal activity recognition based on videos, inertial sensors and ambient sensors from the smart home, on their own or fused to each other. The classification DL framework has also validated on our dataset and on the University of Texas at Dallas Multimodal Human Activities Dataset (UTD-MHAD), a widely used benchmark for activity recognition based on videos and inertial sensors, providing a comparative analysis between the results on the two datasets considered. Results demonstrate that the introduction of data from ambient sensors expressively improved the accuracy results.

candidates.title: Maize tassel detection from UAV imagery using deep learning
candidates.description: Dataset associated with paper titled "Maize Tassel Detection from UAV Imagery Using Deep Learning" published on the journal of Frontiers in Robotics and AI (DOI: 10.3389/frobt.2021.600410). The timing of flowering plays a critical role in determining the productivity of agricultural crops. If the crops flower too early, the crop would mature before the end of the growing season, losing the opportunity to capture and use large amounts of light energy. If the crops flower too late, the crop may be killed by the change of seasons before it is ready to harvest. Maize flowering is one of the most important periods where even small amounts of stress can significantly alter yield. In this work, we developed and compared two methods for automatic tassel detection based on the imagery collected from an unmanned aerial vehicle, using deep learning models. The first approach was a customized framework for tassel detection based on convolutional neural network (TD-CNN). The other method was a state-of-the-art object detection technique of the faster region-based CNN (Faster R-CNN), serving as baseline detection accuracy. The evaluation criteria for tassel detection were customized to correctly reflect the needs of tassel detection in an agricultural setting. Although detecting thin tassels in the aerial imagery is challenging, our results showed promising accuracy: the TD-CNN had an F1 score of 95.9% and the Faster R-CNN had 97.9% F1 score. More CNN-based model structures can be investigated in the future for improved accuracy, speed, and generalizability on aerial-based tassel detection. The dataset including raw images and labelled images are here. The code are available on Dr. Aziza Alzadjali's GitHub account "azizanajeeb" (github.com).
